shows.title: Nymphäum
shows.description:
Anselm Kiefer turns the vast industrial halls of Thaddaeus Ropac's Pantin outpost into a painterly sanctuary dedicated to nymphs, the minor deities of springs, rivers and groves in classical mythology. Across more than twenty new paintings, some spanning many meters of canvas, he layers lead, straw, gold leaf, shellac and the jade-toned residue of electrolysis into surfaces so thick they read almost as topography. Bathing figures dissolve into dark water, faces emerge camouflaged among foliage, and in the exhibition's most staggering work, a nearly eight-meter-wide vision of mountain nymphs, Kiefer reworks a nineteenth-century academic painting into something bleaker and more geological.

What makes the show compelling isn't just its scale, which is considerable even by Kiefer's own monumental standards, but the way it braids together two of his oldest preoccupations: the classical past as a wound that keeps reopening, and the natural world's slow reconquest of ruined, man-made terrain. Some canvases replace his familiar scorched landscapes with glowing city grids inspired by light through the trees of Central Park, their windows built from meticulous gold leaf, while vines and collaged straw seem to physically pierce through from behind, as if nature were clawing back the frame itself.

Kiefer has spent more than five decades turning myth, alchemy and the trauma of European history into material fact, and Nymphäum feels like a late, ambitious chapter in that project. It's a demanding show, dense with reference and sheer physical weight, but it rewards close looking: the closer you get to these surfaces, the more they seem to move.

shows.title: Virgin Turns (Virages Vierges)
shows.description:
Pauline Curnier Jardin builds immersive, slightly unhinged worlds out of video, fabric sculpture and performance, and this survey at Palais de Tokyo is the biggest showcase of her work to date in France. The title plays on a double meaning: virgins as female bodies loaded with centuries of sanctification and suspicion, saints and sinners at once, and virgin territory as unmapped ground where new stories can take root. Both readings run through the show's tented, womb-like installations and looping video works, where ritual, camp theatrics and documentary footage bleed into each other without much regard for hierarchy.

The centerpiece is a new video installation inspired by a real clandestine cinema discovered in 2004 in tunnels beneath the Trocadéro, practically underneath the museum itself, a detail that gives the whole show a nice sense of digging into buried, dissident histories literally on its own doorstep. Elsewhere, large fabric structures recall crumbling amphitheaters and reliquaries, staging her recurring interest in bodily vulnerability, popular spirituality and the theater of femininity.

Curnier Jardin has been circling these ideas for years in group shows at Palais de Tokyo and in major presentations at Hamburger Bahnhof and elsewhere, but Virgin Turns is her fullest statement yet, and it's being organized in partnership with the Reina Sofía in Madrid, which will host its own version in 2027. It's an odd, immersive, occasionally overwhelming show, well suited to a museum that has always made room for art on the edge of spectacle.

shows.title: Les Chiens de Pavlov (Pavlov's Dogs)
shows.description:
Johan Creten has spent nearly forty years reestablishing ceramics as a serious contemporary medium, working his way through studios in Mexico, Rome, Miami and The Hague before settling into La Solfatara, the shared Montreuil studio he keeps with Jean-Michel Othoniel. This new show at Perrotin's Marais space starts from an unusually personal object: a stack of obsolete computer towers inherited from his father, a lifelong devotee of new technology, which Creten piles up like ruins and treats as a monument to a certain kind of faith in progress that has visibly aged.

Around that installation, the exhibition fills out with the vocabulary Creten is best known for: glazed stoneware and bronze creatures, drawings, and recurring figures like his condor and Danaé, cast here in new material or new scale. The title nods to Pavlov's conditioning experiments, and Creten uses it to prod at reflex and automatism, how quickly certain images or objects trigger a response before we've thought about why. A section given over to the seven virtues slows the pace back down, working as counterweight to the show's more anxious, tech-fossil energy.

It's a free, walk-in show and a good entry point into Creten's work if you don't know it: playful in material, but with real unease underneath about memory, obsolescence, and what we choose to keep believing in.
